query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the EAM reference potential in TOR-TILD with a deep learning interatomic potential trained on ab initio liquid and solid configurations will significantly reduce the thermodynamic integration path mismatch by enhancing phase-space overlap across the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid.
generation.material_initial_state: A multicomponent high-entropy alloy (e.g., a refractory carbide or a tungsten-based HEA) in its solid state near its high melting temperature, with an ab initio molecular dynamics ensemble of atomic configurations representing the liquid state.
generation.intervention: Integrate a deep learning potential (e.g., a deep neural network trained on ab initio energies and forces from a large set of liquid and near-liquid configurations) into the TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration framework as the reference potential.
generation.conditions: High temperatures near the melting point (approximately 3000–4000 K for refractory HEAs), with compositions spanning multicomponent systems such as (TiZrTaHfNb)-based alloys, where configurational diversity is critical.
generation.structural_mediator: The deep learning potential, by accurately reproducing local atomic environments and many-body interactions, serves as an intermediate representation bridging the ab initio target free energy landscape and the reference state used in integration.
generation.mechanism: By training directly on ab initio data, the ML potential captures the extensive variety of atomic configurations (both vibrational and configurational contributions) present in the disordered liquid phase, thereby enhancing phase-space overlap. This reduces the mismatch in the thermodynamic integration path relative to when using a conventional EAM potential.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch that, based on prior deep learning potential studies, may lead to error reductions on the order of tens of meV/atom compared to TOR-TILD calculations with EAM references. This improvement should yield more accurate free energy estimates and melting temperature predictions.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD free energy integration performed with conventional EAM reference potentials, which suffer from significant phase-space mismatches in representing the ab initio liquid state.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to be most significant for HEAs with high configurational complexity at temperatures near their melting point; extreme compositions or conditions with insufficient ab initio training data might limit the effectiveness of the ML potential.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative reduction in path mismatch (e.g., magnitude in meV/atom improvement) is approximate and may vary with the quality and range of the training data; additional studies are needed to establish error bars and assess transferability across different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Implement the deep learning potential-based TOR-TILD simulation for a chosen multicomponent HEA near its melting temperature alongside a control simulation using a conventional EAM potential. Perform parallel free energy integrations while systematically varying the training data set and temperature conditions.
measurements: Compare the computed free energy differences along the integration path.
Evaluate the predicted melting temperatures against high-fidelity ab initio benchmarks from elemental or binary systems.
Assess the phase-space overlap quantitatively via configurational sampling metrics and error estimates in free energy (meV/atom).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deep learning potential fails to reduce the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by a statistically significant margin (e.g., error reduction less than anticipated relative to the EAM reference) or yields free energy predictions that do not converge closer to known ab initio/experimental benchmarks, the hypothesis would be falsified.

papers.title: Melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides by deep learning potentials.
papers.system: High-entropy carbonitrides (e.g., (TiZrTaHfNb)C variants) in both solid and liquid states near melting temperatures
papers.approach: Replacement of conventional empirical potentials (EAM) with deep learning interatomic potentials to simulate melting via a two‐phase method
papers.findings: The deep learning potentials capture a broad ensemble of atomic configurations, yielding robust estimates of melting temperatures (with quantified errors in superheating and supercooling) and indicating a potential reduction in the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to approaches based on EAM references.
papers.mechanism: By training directly on ab initio data, the deep learning potentials offer higher fidelity in representing many-body interactions and configurational disorder of the liquid, thereby improving the overlap between the ab initio target and the reference phase-space.

papers.title: Vibrational Entropy of Crystalline Solids from Covariance of Atomic Displacements.
papers.system: Elemental metals (e.g., BCC sodium and FCC aluminum) and extension to a high-entropy alloy
papers.approach: AIMD simulations combined with covariance analysis of atomic displacements to compute vibrational (and by extension configurational) entropy
papers.findings: The method captures many-body correlations yielding entropy values in good agreement with experiments above the Debye temperatures; this demonstrates the viability of using ab initio ensembles to represent diverse atomic configurations.
papers.mechanism: The calculation of entropy from the full N-body distribution improves the representation of configurational space, suggesting that methods which incorporate many-body correlations (similar to ML potentials) can bridge gaps left by simpler EAM models.

papers.title: Ab initio framework for deciphering trade-off relationships in multi-component alloys.
papers.approach: Integration of advanced ab initio techniques with machine learning interatomic potentials and coherent-potential approximation to model phase stability and property trade-offs
papers.findings: The framework successfully predicts mechanical and thermodynamic properties over a broad composition space, demonstrating that enhancing the representation of configurational complexity (via ML potentials) yields better predictions than models reliant on traditional potentials.
papers.mechanism: The use of machine learning potentials better captures the diversity of atomic configurations compared to empirical potentials like EAM. This enhanced configurational sampling improves phase-space overlap in thermodynamic integrations.

established: EAM potentials have limitations in representing the full complexity and configurational entropy of the ab initio liquid state in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Configurational and vibrational contributions to free energy play critical roles at high temperatures, especially near the melting point.
Recent advances in machine learning (deep learning, moment tensor potentials) have provided promising alternatives by offering a more flexible and accurate description of many-body interactions.

approaches_tried.approach: Use of Embedded-Atom Method (EAM) references within TOR-TILD for thermodynamic integration
approaches_tried.outcome: Encountered significant reference–target phase-space mismatch due to an inability to represent the vast number of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid, leading to errors in free energy integration.

approaches_tried.approach: Implementing deep learning/machine learning interatomic potentials trained on ab initio data
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved phase-space overlap and reduced thermodynamic-integration path mismatch, as evidenced by more accurate and lower-error predictions of melting temperatures.

mechanisms: Increasing the fidelity of the interatomic potential by capturing many-body effects and configurational disorder directly improves reference–target phase-space overlap.
Machine learning potentials, by being trained to reproduce ab initio energies across many configurations, lower the mismatch in the thermodynamic integration pathway compared to EAM references.
Enhanced configurational sampling directly addresses the excessive diversity of atomic arrangements in the liquid state that traditional EAM forms cannot capture.
disagreements: There is debate over the relative importance of vibrational versus configurational entropy contributions at high temperatures, which impacts the choice of reference potential.

Some studies question whether advanced ML potentials always outperform well-tuned empirical potentials in every thermodynamic integration context, particularly regarding computational cost versus accuracy.
open_questions: Quantitatively, how much can the replacement of EAM with ML potentials reduce the thermodynamic integration path mismatch in TOR-TILD calculations?
What are the precise composition and temperature ranges (e.g., in terms of melting temperature windows ~3000–4000 K for certain HEAs) where this intervention yields the most significant improvement?
Can the new ML-based approach be conclusively benchmarked against experimental melting/free-energy data, particularly in elemental or binary systems, to falsify alternative hypotheses?
opportunities: Implement the single methodological intervention of replacing EAM reference potentials with machine-learned potentials (such as deep neural network or moment tensor potentials) in the TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration framework.

Apply this intervention to multicomponent high-entropy alloys, especially those relevant to ultra-high temperature applications (e.g., refractory carbides, tungsten-based HEAs), to comprehensively map the improved performance across composition and temperature ranges.

Conduct decisive free-energy benchmarking by comparing the predicted free energy differences at melting (or along the integration path) with high-fidelity ab initio calculations and experimental measurements from well-understood elemental and binary systems.

directions.direction: Replace the traditional EAM reference potential within TOR-TILD with a deep learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is trained directly on extensive ab initio data from both solid and liquid configurations at high melting temperatures.
directions.assessment: This strategy directly targets the limited configurational representation of EAM by leveraging ML approaches that capture many‐body interactions and diverse liquid configurations. It is supported by recent evidence showing improved phase‐space overlap and reduced integration path mismatch in high-entropy systems (see record_ids PMC11576752::web::017 and PMC11275555::web::000). The physics is well understood from ab initio training data and the approach is computationally feasible with current ML methods.

directions.direction: Integrate actively-learned moment tensor potentials (MTPs) into TOR-TILD to serve as adaptive reference potentials, dynamically refined to capture the broad distribution of liquid configurations.
directions.assessment: While similar in principle to MLIPs, moment tensor potentials with active learning provide an iterative refinement scheme that could further reduce path mismatch. However, the complexity of active learning in strongly disordered liquid phases may pose additional computational overhead. Physics supports the many-body nature and feasibility is moderate with emerging frameworks.

directions.direction: Augment the EAM reference by incorporating ensemble averaging over a large set of pre-computed high-temperature ab initio liquid configurations, effectively creating a composite potential.
directions.assessment: This approach attempts to salvage the EAM framework by statistical sampling of many configurations. It directly attacks the configurational diversity issue but might still be limited by the functional form of EAM. Although conceptually straightforward, it relies on post-processing corrections rather than an intrinsic potential representation.

directions.direction: Develop a multiscale hybrid method that couples EAM potentials with explicit AIMD-based corrections (e.g., via covariance analysis of atomic displacements) to account for many-body effects in the liquid phase.
directions.assessment: This intervention uses ab initio molecular dynamics to compute corrections for the reference free energy. It supports physics through vibrational and configurational entropy evaluation (see record_id PMC9141984::web::001) but is more indirect and computationally intensive, potentially reducing its feasibility compared to direct ML potential replacement.

directions.direction: Employ a modified thermodynamic integration scheme that utilizes direct sampling from high-temperature AIMD trajectories to evaluate the free energy, bypassing the need for a traditional empirical reference potential altogether.
directions.assessment: This methodology circumvents the limitations of EAM by using ab initio sampling directly. While it would yield highly accurate free energies, the computational cost at high melting temperatures for multicomponent HEAs makes it challenging for routine application. It is supported by evidence that emphasizes the importance of configurational sampling but may be less feasible for extensive alloy screening.

choice.direction: Replace the traditional EAM reference potential within TOR-TILD with a deep learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on ab initio data.
choice.why: This approach directly overcomes the EAM limitations by inherently capturing the vast configurational space through learning many-body interactions. It improves reference–target phase-space overlap, is supported by recent successes in high-entropy materials (PMC11576752::web::017, PMC11275555::web::000) and melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides, and is computationally feasible using state-of-the-art deep learning frameworks.
